title: Synthetic Data -- Anonymisation Groundhog Day
summary: Measures the privacy gain of publishing synthetic data by running the same linkage and attribute-inference games against synthetic datasets and against traditionally sanitised releases, and concludes that synthetic data either fails to stop the attacks or loses the utility it was meant to preserve, with the gain varying so widely from record to record that it cannot be promised in advance. CTGAN is one of the five generative models the attacks are run against, and is the deep tabular generator carried through the headline per-record results.
evidence: section 2.1 (Generative models in this study) lists CTGAN alongside IndHist, BayNet, PrivBay and PATEGAN and describes it as using mode-specific normalisation of attributes plus a conditional generator with training-by-sampling for imbalanced datasets; Figure 2 reports expected per-record privacy gain for IndHist, BayNet and CTGAN on the Texas and Adult datasets under three feature sets, and the accompanying text records one outlier target receiving a gain below 0.005 from CTGAN-trained synthetic data; Table 2 in appendix 8.1 gives the CTGAN hyperparameters used (embeddings 128, gen_dim and dis_dim of (256,256), l2scale 1e-6); SDGym at sdv.dev appears in the bibliography as an existing benchmarking framework but is not run

title: DTGAN: Differential Private Training for Tabular GANs
summary: Asks where differential privacy should be enforced in a tabular GAN, and answers it by building two variants of DTGAN that apply DP-SGD with subsampled Renyi accounting to the discriminator and to the generator respectively, showing that noising the discriminator gives the better utility-privacy trade-off and that DP-SGD outperforms the PATE framework on three datasets against PATE-GAN and DP-WGAN. CTGAN's conditional architecture is what the generator-side privacy argument rests on: the generator loss is described as a by-product of that architecture, which makes the conditional vector independent of the real training data, but CTGAN itself is neither run nor compared against.
evidence: section 3.1 states that the generator loss is a by-product of the conditional architecture and is used to ensure the generator respects the conditional constraints imposed during training, citing Xu et al. (2019); section 3.3 repeats this to establish that the generator loss depends only on the conditional vector sampled at random and is therefore independent of the real training data, which is the premise of Corollary 2; section 4.1 names the baselines as PATE-GAN and DP-WGAN only, and Tables 3-5 report no CTGAN row; the CTAB-GAN reference appears in the bibliography alone
needs: convention gap: CTGAN's conditional architecture is a structural component of the proposed model and load-bearing for its privacy proof, yet CTGAN is never named in prose, run, or benchmarked. Recorded citation_only 2 under the adopted-but-not-run rule; an inherited-architecture convention, if one is wanted, would place this higher

title: Synthesising Electronic Health Records: Cystic Fibrosis Patient Group
summary: Synthesises cystic fibrosis electronic health records from the IBM Explorys dataset to address class imbalance in mortality-risk prediction, and evaluates four generators on authenticity, fidelity and diversity before using their samples to augment the minority class, finding that augmentation improves two of four downstream models while trading against similarity to the real records. CTGAN is one of the four compared generators, implemented from the architecture and code repository of Xu et al. (2019), and its behaviour on duplication, precision, density and coverage is reported alongside the variational autoencoder and the two differentially private GANs.
evidence: the Synthetic Data Generators paragraph in section 3 names the four generators as VAE, DPGAN at two noise levels and CTGAN, and describes CTGAN as addressing sparsity and imbalanced categorical columns by sampling vectors during training and conditioning the generator; the appendix states that CTGAN was implemented by adopting the model architecture provided in Xu et al. (2019) and the corresponding code repo; Figure 1 reports CTGAN duplicating 34 per cent of the training data across 100,000 samples and generating the largest number of unique samples at an average of 33,689; the fidelity paragraph records CTGAN last on precision (0.37) and density (0.13) but highest on recall (0.67), with coverage degrading to 0.31

title: A Constructive GAN-based Approach to Exact Estimate Treatment Effect without Matching
summary: Replaces the matching step in counterfactual inference with a generative one: two conditional GANs learn the joint densities of the treatment and control groups, conditional average treatment effects are read off as the difference between the two conditional densities at the same covariate value, and their ensemble average over the treated sample is the estimate of the average treatment effect on the treated, which sidesteps the sample dropping and lack of common support that matching suffers in high dimensions. CTGAN is the generator the estimator is built on, taken from its Python code as documented on sdv.dev and run with a single merged network conditioned on a treatment one-hot vector in place of two separate ones.
evidence: section 3.3 states that to make the estimator applicable to tabular economic datasets the training proceeds through CTGAN as proposed by Xu et al. (2019), crediting its conditional generator and training-by-sampling algorithm for handling mixed continuous and discrete inputs; the following paragraph says the joint densities are learned by a method equivalent to CTGAN's Python code, with footnote 2 pointing at https://sdv.dev/SDV/user_guides/single_table/ctgan.html, and that the only difference from the original method is merging two separate GANs into one trained by distinguishing a one-hot input vector, done to save computing resources; section 5 reports that CTGAN's own evaluation criteria including KL distance and KS statistic can fail at high covariate dimension, which the authors work around by re-running training with adjusted hyperparameters and layer scales

title: Masked Language Modeling Becomes Conditional Density Estimation for Tabular Data Synthesis
summary: Recasts masked language modelling over discretised tabular columns as histogram-based non-parametric conditional density estimation, showing that minimising the multi-class classification loss corresponds to minimising a divergence between the true and modelled conditional densities, which yields MaCoDE as a single model that generates across arbitrary combinations of target and conditional variables, supports multiple imputation under several missingness mechanisms, and tunes privacy by a sampling temperature without retraining. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the seven compared generators, run from the sdv-dev repository at default hyperparameters with the latent dimension aligned to 100 for a fair size comparison.
evidence: section 2 lists CTGAN and TVAE (both Xu et al. 2019) first among the deep generative baselines; the Baseline models paragraph in section 4 names them for research questions Q1 and Q2; the implementation appendix states that the CTGAN and TVAE implementations follow the official repository with default hyperparameters and the latent dimension adjusted to 100, with footnote 4 giving https://github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN; the fidelity and utility table reports CTGAN and TVAE rows against MaCoDE on KL, goodness-of-fit, MMD, Wasserstein, SMAPE, F1 and model and feature selection scores

title: Preserving logical and functional dependencies in synthetic tabular data
summary: Introduces the notion of logical dependency between attributes alongside the existing notion of functional dependency, gives a Q-score that quantifies it, and uses that measure to test whether generators reproduce the dependencies present in the real table, concluding that none of the models examined preserves both reliably on small datasets. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the seven generators run and scored, and the study describes CTGAN's mode-specific normalisation, its variational Gaussian mixture mode selection, its conditional vector and its training-by-sampling strategy as the design being tested.
evidence: section 2.1 describes CTGAN as incorporating mode-specific normalisation with a variational Gaussian mixture model to model non-Gaussian and multimodal continuous distributions, a conditional vector supplied to the generator alongside noise, and packing to prevent mode collapse, and separately describes TVAE; the workflow in Figure 1 and section 4 state that synthetic data was generated with CTGAN, CTABGAN, CTABGAN Plus, TVAE, NextConvGeN, TabDDPM and TabuLa, trained on the complete table rather than a split; Figure 3 charts logical-dependency preservation across those models and the discussion notes that CTGAN, CTABGAN, CTABGAN Plus and TVAE do not always maintain logical connections, with CTGAN comparatively the best of the GAN models

title: TabDiff: a Mixed-type Diffusion Model for Tabular Data Generation
summary: Models numerical and categorical columns in a single joint continuous-time diffusion process with per-feature learnable noise schedules, parameterised by a transformer and trained end to end, and adds a stochastic sampler that restarts the forward process at each denoising step, reporting gains over eight generators on shape, trend, downstream utility and detection. CTGAN and TVAE are the GAN and VAE baselines in that comparison, appearing as rows in the fidelity and utility tables.
evidence: section 3 groups the related work and names TVAE (Xu et al. 2019) among the VAE-based methods and CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) among the GAN-based ones as lacking expressivity for complicated distributions; the Baselines paragraph in section 4.1 lists CTGAN as the GAN-based method and TVAE as one of the VAE-based methods among the eight compared; Tables 1 and 2 report CTGAN and TVAE error rates for shape and trend across Adult, Default, Shoppers, Magic, Beijing, News and Diabetes, with a footnote recording that baseline results other than on Diabetes are taken from Zhang et al. (2024) rather than re-run
